contribution: The last unit of the French chapter: beginners read an original A2–B1 news text about the WEST record at Cadarache and the ITER worksite, discover that partial comprehension is possible through names, numbers, look-alike words in English, Swedish and Finnish, word endings and context, learn the common false friends (actuel, expérience, milliard), and transfer the strategies to a second short text.
learn: find the topic and the main facts of a short French news text without a dictionary.
use look-alike words in English, Swedish and Finnish, word endings and the context to work out new words.
recognise false friends: French words that look like English ones but mean something else.
prior: The CEA, Cadarache and ITER (chapter *At a research centre in Provence*)

activities.text: On the last morning of your (imagined) visit, you have breakfast in a café in Manosque. Someone has left the regional newspaper on the table. On the science page you see the words *tokamak*, *Cadarache* and *ITER*. You have studied French for a few weeks, and you have no dictionary with you.
activities.question: Can you find out what the article says, and how?

activities.text:
Sentence starters

  • When I read a text in a language I do not know well, I first …
  • A French word I understood because of English or Swedish is …
  • I think I will understand …, but not …

activities.title: Think about it: reading in a language you hardly know
activities.prompt: Have you ever understood something in a language you have not studied: a sign abroad, a menu, a German or Spanish product label? What helped you? Then look at these French words and say what they mean: la température, un réacteur, international, la physique, un kilomètre.
activities.pair: Discuss with a partner for three minutes, then write your answer together.
activities.model: On a trip we understood signs and menus because many words looked like English or Swedish words, because of pictures and numbers, and because we knew what kind of text it was (a timetable, a menu). The French words mean temperature, a reactor, international, physics and a kilometre: they look almost the same in English, and Swedish and Finnish have similar words (*temperatur*, *reaktor*, *fysiikka*, *kilometri*).
criteria: We name at least two things that help: look-alike words, numbers, pictures, the type of text.
We give the meaning of the five French words.
We notice that Swedish or Finnish have similar words too.

activities.title: Prediction 1: how much will you understand?
activities.prompt: You will read a French news text of about 190 words, with no dictionary and five minutes of time. How much do you think you will understand? Commit now; your reading and the theory summary will show you.

choices.text: The topic and the main facts
choices.feedback: This is what most beginners manage: names, numbers and international words carry the topic and most of the facts. The theory shows why: thousands of French words have relatives in English, Swedish and Finnish.

choices.text: Almost nothing: I hardly speak French
choices.feedback: Speaking and reading are different skills. Names, dates, numbers and look-alike words (*record*, *physiciens*, *projet*) give most readers the topic and the main facts even after a few weeks of French.
A few words have no look-alike (*aimants*, *chantier*) and some grammar is new, so word-by-word comprehension is unlikely. But you do not need it: the topic and the main facts are enough.

choices.text: Only the names of people and places
choices.feedback: You will understand much more than names: numbers, dates and many look-alike words (*record*, *physiciens*, *projet*) carry the facts.

activities.title: Prediction 2: a look-alike
activities.prompt: The text ends with « Selon le calendrier actuel … ». What does *actuel* mean? Commit now; the theory summary will show you.

choices.feedback: Right: *actuel* is a false friend. Le calendrier actuel is the current schedule, and actuellement means *currently*, not *actually*.
This is the trap: *actuel* looks like *actual*, but it means *current*. Le calendrier actuel is the current schedule.
*Actuel* is not related to *active* here: it means *current*. Le calendrier actuel is the schedule as it is now.
A schedule should be accurate, but that is not what the word says. *Actuel* means *current*: the schedule as it is now.

activities.title: Step 1: a first look (two minutes)
activities.text:
Read only the title, the place, the names and every number. Do not read the sentences yet. Then answer the question below.

Fusion nucléaire : record de durée à Cadarache

Saint-Paul-lez-Durance (Bouches-du-Rhône). Le 12 février 2025, les physiciens du CEA ont battu un record mondial. Dans leur tokamak WEST, installé au centre de Cadarache, ils ont maintenu un plasma pendant 1 337 secondes, soit plus de 22 minutes. C'est 25 % de plus que le record précédent, obtenu en Chine quelques semaines plus tôt.

Un plasma est un gaz très chaud, à plusieurs dizaines de millions de degrés. Aucun matériau ne résiste à cette température : la machine utilise donc des aimants très puissants pour garder le plasma loin des parois.

Selon les chercheurs, ce résultat est important pour ITER, le grand projet international construit juste à côté. Sept membres participent au projet : la Chine, l'Union européenne, l'Inde, le Japon, la Corée, la Russie et les États-Unis. Leur objectif : produire 500 mégawatts de puissance de fusion avec seulement 50 mégawatts de chauffage. Attention : ITER ne produira pas d'électricité. C'est une expérience scientifique.

Le chantier avance. En juillet 2026, les équipes ont installé le sixième des neuf modules qui forment le cœur de la machine, avec presque six mois d'avance sur le calendrier. Selon le calendrier actuel, les premières expériences scientifiques commenceront en 2034.

*The text was written for this course in the style of a newspaper; the facts were checked against the CEA, EUROfusion and ITER in November 2026.*

activities.title: What is the text about?
activities.prompt: From the title, the names and the numbers only: what is the text about?

choices.text: A fusion record and ITER's progress
choices.feedback: Yes. Record, WEST, 1 337 secondes, ITER, 2026 and 2034 already give you the topic: a long plasma at Cadarache and the ITER worksite.

choices.text: A new fusion power station in Provence
choices.feedback: The text speaks of a tokamak and of ITER, which *ne produira pas d'électricité*. It is a scientific record and a worksite, not a power station.

choices.text: An accident at a research centre
choices.feedback: Nothing in the title or the numbers suggests an accident: *record*, *secondes* and *projet* point to a scientific success and a building project.

choices.text: A meeting of seven heads of state
choices.feedback: Seven countries and the EU are named, but as ITER's members, not at a meeting. The title speaks of a *record* at Cadarache.

activities.title: Step 2: hunt for look-alikes
activities.text: Now read the sentences. Underline in your head (or on paper) every word that looks like a word you know in English, Swedish or Finnish. Then work out the words below.

activities.title: Step 3: read for detail

sections: Why you understand more than you think

activities.title: Back to your predictions
activities.prompt: Compare your two predictions with what happened when you read, and with the theory. Then answer the opening question in English in one or two sentences: why can you understand a French news text about fusion after only a few weeks of French?

activities.title: Look-alike, false friend or context?
Tell a friend what the text says
activities.text:
Word bank

a record, a plasma, a tokamak, the CEA, Cadarache, ITER, next door, the members, fusion power, heating power, no electricity, a scientific experiment, the worksite, ahead of schedule, research operation

Sentence starters

  • The text is about …
  • On 12 February 2025, …
  • The record matters for ITER because …
  • The text also says that ITER …
  • I understood … because the word looks like …

activities.title: Write: the text in English
activities.prompt: A friend who does not read French asks what the article says. Write a summary in English in four or five sentences: what happened, where and when, why it matters for ITER, and what the text says about ITER's progress.
activities.pair: Tell your partner first, in English, without looking at the text; then write the summary together.
activities.model: On 12 February 2025, physicists of the French CEA kept a plasma in their tokamak WEST at Cadarache for 1,337 seconds, more than 22 minutes. This was a world record, 25 % longer than a record set in China a few weeks before. The machine uses strong magnets to keep the very hot plasma away from the walls. The researchers say the result matters for ITER, the international project next door, which aims to produce 500 MW of fusion power from 50 MW of heating but will not produce electricity. In July 2026 six of the nine core modules of ITER were installed, almost six months ahead of schedule, and research operation is planned to start in 2034.
criteria: The summary gives what happened, where and when (WEST, Cadarache, 12 February 2025, over 22 minutes).
It explains the link to ITER and says that ITER will not produce electricity.
It includes ITER's progress (six of nine modules in July 2026, start in 2034) with correct numbers.
The English is clear, and the facts are not changed or invented.

activities.title: A second text: your turn
activities.text:
Use the five strategies on a second, shorter text, also written for this course. Read it once for the topic, then once for detail.

Manosque : une école internationale pour les familles d'ITER

À Manosque, à une quinzaine de kilomètres d'ITER, une école internationale accueille les enfants des familles qui travaillent sur le projet. Elle a ouvert en 2007 avec 130 élèves de 3 à 18 ans. L'enseignement est bilingue : l'école a six sections linguistiques et une section européenne. La France s'était engagée à créer cette école quand ITER a choisi la Provence.

activities.title: What does the second text say?
activities.prompt: Write in English, in two or three sentences, what the second text says. Then list four French words you understood because of a look-alike, and one you worked out from the context.
activities.model: In Manosque, about fifteen kilometres from ITER, an international school teaches the children of families who work on the project. It opened in 2007 with 130 pupils aged 3 to 18, teaches in two languages and has six language sections and a European section. France promised to create the school when ITER chose Provence. Look-alikes: internationale, familles, bilingue, sections linguistiques, européenne. From the context: élèves (pupils), because the school has 130 of them, aged 3 to 18.
criteria: I give the topic: an international school in Manosque for ITER families.
I include at least two facts with numbers (2007, 130 pupils, ages 3–18, six sections).
I list four look-alike words and one word from the context, with their meaning.

activities.title: Extension: real French news
activities.text: Find a real French text about fusion or ITER: the French pages of iter.org, the CEA's news, or a French newspaper. Choose a short article or the first paragraph of a longer one. Use the five strategies, write its topic and three facts in English, and note where and when it was published. Tell another pair what you found.

activities.title: 1. A false friend
activities.prompt: A French news text says: « Actuellement, 5 000 personnes travaillent sur le site. » What does *actuellement* mean?

choices.feedback: Yes: *actuellement* is a false friend. The sentence says that about 5,000 people work on the site at present.
This is the trap: *actuellement* looks like *actually*, but it means *currently*. *Actually* is en fait in French.
*Actuellement* is about now: *currently*. *Finally* is finalement.
The number is a round figure, but the word means *currently*, at present. *Exactly* is exactement.

activities.title: 2. A big number
activities.prompt: A French article says that a project costs « plusieurs milliards d'euros ». What does *un milliard* mean?

choices.feedback: Yes: *un milliard* is a thousand million, the English *billion* (Swedish *miljard*, Finnish *miljardi*).
A million is un million. *Un milliard* is a thousand times more: $10^{9}$, a billion.
That is the French *un billion*, another false friend. *Un milliard* is $10^{9}$, a billion.
A thousand is mille. *Un milliard* is $10^{9}$, a billion: Swedish *miljard*, Finnish *miljardi*.

activities.title: 3. An unknown word
activities.prompt: In a French text you meet *les aimants*, and it looks like no word you know. What is the best first step?

choices.text: Read on and use the context.
choices.feedback: Yes. The sentence says the *aimants* are very strong and keep the hot plasma away from the walls: they must be magnets. Context often solves a word.

choices.text: Stop reading until you look it up.
choices.feedback: Looking a word up is fine later, but stopping at every word loses the meaning of the text. Read on first: the context shows that *aimants* are magnets.

choices.text: Decide it means *aims*, as it looks.
choices.feedback: A guess from the spelling alone can mislead: *aimants* has nothing to do with *aims*. The context (strong, keeping plasma from the walls) shows they are magnets.
Skipping one word can be fine, but not the whole paragraph: it has the key facts. Read on, and the context shows that *aimants* are magnets.

activities.title: 4. Write: how I read French
activities.prompt: Explain to a classmate who starts French next year how to read a short French text without a dictionary. Name three strategies and give one example of each from today's texts (four to six sentences, in English).
activities.model: First read the title, the names and the numbers: *Cadarache*, *WEST*, *12 février 2025* and *1 337 secondes* already tell you that the text is about a record. Then look for words that look like English, Swedish or Finnish words, such as *physiciens* (physicists, *fysiker*) or *projet* (project, *projekti*). When a word looks like nothing you know, read on and use the context: *aimants* keep a very hot plasma away from the walls, so they must be magnets. Be careful with false friends: *actuel* means current, not actual.
criteria: Each strategy has a correct example from the texts.
I mention false friends or checking a guess against the context.
My explanation is clear enough for a beginner to follow.
